The other growth interventions (Two-Speed, Moment Transplant, GradMax, Net2Wider) provide less consistent gains across this benchmark suite, with some helping in one benchmark but not others. The diversity of the benchmarks (input shift, concept shift, alternating difficulty, non-repeating tasks) strengthens the claim that the pattern is general and not an artifact of a single shift type.

metadata.credit: This strength supports the conclusion that PRUNE is reliable under rapid shift and that GROW+Rand. Smooth-Leaky is the most robust growth variant. The evaluation across five diverse failure out benchmarks with different shift dynamics guards against overfitting to a single challenge. The consistent pattern—PRUNE strong when edits are rapid, GROW+RSL narrowing the gap and becoming strongest when integration time is available—provides converging evidence for the time-scale interpretation of growth’s viability. Without this multi-benchmark evaluation, each individual benchmark could be attributed to a specific artifact (e.g., Permuted MNIST is easy, Random Label CIFAR is near random). The scope of credit is a generalization-scope underwriting: the pattern is not confined to one dataset or shift type, and the relative ordering of methods is broadly repeatable across the suite.

nodes.title: Consistent pattern across five diverse plasticity-stressing benchmarks

steps.reasoning: The paper introduces a 3-layer fully-connected MLP backbone with two masked hidden layers (each of size $H=256$) and an unmasked 10-way classifier head. Hidden unit activity is controlled by binary masks $m^{(\ell)} \in \{0,1\}^{d_\ell}$ per layer $\ell$, defined as: $h^{(\ell)} = \phi(z^{(\ell)}) \odot m^{(\ell)}$, where $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication.

The paper defines three model families under matched data streams, optimizers, and compactness targets: Dense (no sparsification), Prune (Iterative Magnitude Pruning with IMP-style rewind, following the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis protocol), and Grow (start from a sparse seed mask and iteratively activate units using an activation-frequency heuristic based on the fraction of post-activation values exceeding a small threshold $\tau=0.05$ on a mini-batch). For Grow, masks are updated in place with no rewind. Both Grow and Prune proceed through sequential structural-edit cycles until reaching a final target retained compactness $c \in \{20, 30, 40, 50\}\%$.

The paper evaluates three benchmark settings: (i) IID MNIST, (ii) class-incremental Split-MNIST with a single shared 10-way head and TinyER replay buffer (50 samples per class), and (iii) class-incremental Split-Fashion-MNIST with TinyER. Training uses SGD with learning rate $\eta=0.01$. All methods share the same training horizon. Winning-Ticket evaluation freezes the final mask, reinitializes weights, and retrains from scratch following the standard LTH protocol.
[13]

Results are reported in Table 1 and Table 3 (compactness-resolved). On IID MNIST, Grow and Prune produce closely matched Winning-Ticket final accuracy (WT Final) and trajectory-average accuracy (WT TAA) across compactness budgets $c \in \{20,30,40,50\}\%$ with no consistent ordering. For example, at c=20% on IID MNIST, Grow WT Final is 95.39±0.13 and Prune WT Final is 95.33±0.12; at c=50%, Grow WT Final is 96.40±0.07 and Prune WT Final is 96.39±0.09. The same pattern holds for Split-MNIST with TinyER (e.g., at c=20%: Grow WT Final 84.53±0.77, Prune WT Final 84.53±0.72; at c=50%: Grow 85.81±0.49, Prune 85.20±0.79) and Split-Fashion-MNIST with TinyER (e.g., at c=20%: Grow WT Final 74.88±1.07, Prune 75.53±1.57; at c=50%: Grow 75.11±2.03, Prune 75.00±1.48). Trajectory-average accuracies are similarly close.

The paper further examines the delta between Winning-Ticket Final accuracy and Cycle Final accuracy ($\Delta_{\text{WT-C}} = \text{Final}_{\text{WT}} - \text{Final}_{\text{Cycle}}$). On IID MNIST, both methods show negative deltas (e.g., at c=20%: Grow -1.16±0.17, Prune -0.63±0.20), indicating the cycle procedure reaches a higher endpoint than the retrained ticket. On the class-incremental settings, both methods show positive deltas (e.g., at c=20% Split-MNIST: Grow +11.15±1.66, Prune +8.52±2.14), reflecting the instability of the online structural-edit trajectory under continual accumulation. In all cases, the two methods remain closely matched.

The paper concludes that across these small MLP benchmarks with IID and class-incremental training, Grow and Prune produce closely matched winning-ticket final accuracy and trajectory-average accuracy with no consistent ordering. This shows that the GROW-PRUNE asymmetry is not inherent to sparsity or class-incremental training regimes and only becomes visible in harder feature-learning settings.

The paper moves to a hybrid ConvNet architecture for CIFAR-100 (and CIFAR-10; App. B.6) to test whether the GROW-PRUNE asymmetry emerges in a harder representation-learning regime. The architecture consists of a dense two-layer convolutional trunk (conv1: 3→32, k=3, p=1, maxpool(2); conv2: 32→64, k=3, p=1, maxpool(2)) followed by a four-layer fully-connected masked head (fc1: 4096→512, fc2: 512→512, fc3: 512→256, fc4: 256→100). Only the hidden layers of the FC head are grown or pruned; the convolutional trunk remains dense for all methods. Structural adaptation is confined to unit-level binary masks $m^{(\ell)} \in \{0,1\}^{d_\ell}$ on FC layers, with activations computed as $h^{(\ell)} = \phi(z^{(\ell)}) \odot m^{(\ell)}$.

Models are trained with SGD ($\eta=0.1$) using cosine annealing over 200 epochs. Structural-edit cycles are divided into 5 cycles, each with 40 epochs per cycle. A neutral allocation schedule distributes the global kept-weight budget proportionally to layer weight mass across the three masked FC layers. ReLU activations are used throughout.

In Cycle evaluation, accuracy is measured at the end of each structural-edit cycle during the Grow/Prune procedure itself, capturing online performance while architecture changes are being made. The final cumulative accuracy after the last structural edit is reported as Cycle-ACC.

Results from Fig. 1(a) and Table 4 show that GROW reaches a stronger Cycle-ACC endpoint than PRUNE at every compactness level. For example, at $c=50\%$, GROW achieves $54.338 \pm 0.221$ while PRUNE achieves $50.227 \pm 0.548$. The gap increases at higher compactness: at $c=20\%$, GROW Cycle-ACC $52.316 \pm 0.317$ vs. PRUNE $47.911 \pm 0.644$; at $c=30\%$, GROW $53.312 \pm 0.247$ vs. PRUNE $49.549 \pm 0.325$; at $c=40\%$, GROW $53.588 \pm 0.313$ vs. PRUNE $49.963 \pm 0.481$.

Welch two-sample t-tests confirm statistical significance across all compactness levels: the GROW vs. PRUNE comparison for Cycle-ACC yields $p < 0.001$ at $c \in \{20,30,40,50\}\%$ (Table 5).

The paper concludes that on CIFAR-100 with a ConvNet architecture, GROW achieves higher Cycle-ACC (endpoint accuracy during the structural-editing procedure) than PRUNE at every compactness level, with the gap increasing at higher compactness.

Using the same CIFAR-100 ConvNet setup (dense convolutional trunk, four-layer FC head, SGD $\eta=0.1$, cosine annealing, 200 epochs, 5 cycles, neutral allocation, ReLU), the paper also evaluates the final masks discovered by GROW and PRUNE under the Winning-Ticket evaluation protocol: freezing the final mask, reinitializing the model weights, and retraining from scratch.

Results from Fig. 1(b) and Table 4 show that after retraining from scratch, GROW and PRUNE produce similar final accuracy across compactness levels. At $c=20\%$, GROW Winning-Ticket ACC is $52.055 \pm 0.324$ and PRUNE is $52.057 \pm 0.283$. At $c=30\%$, GROW is $51.626 \pm 0.232$ and PRUNE is $51.615 \pm 0.280$. At $c=40\%$, GROW is $50.791 \pm 0.338$ and PRUNE is $51.205 \pm 0.415$. At $c=50\%$, GROW is $50.260 \pm 0.257$ and PRUNE is $50.320 \pm 0.415$.

Welch two-sample t-tests (Table 5) indicate that the GROW vs. PRUNE comparison for Winning-Ticket ACC is not statistically significant at any compactness level ($p > 0.05$ at all $c \in \{20,30,40,50\}\%$). PRUNE is slightly stronger at 40-50% compactness, but the difference is not significant.

The paper concludes that the GROW Cycle-ACC advantage observed during structural editing does not translate to clearly superior retrainable sparse architectures. GROW and PRUNE produce similar final accuracy after Winning-Ticket retraining across compactness levels, with no significant difference.

Using the same CIFAR-100 ConvNet setup (dense convolutional trunk, four-layer FC head, SGD $\eta=0.1$, cosine annealing, 200 epochs, 5 cycles, neutral allocation, ReLU), the paper computes trajectory-average accuracy (TAA) as the mean test accuracy across all structural-edit checkpoints. TAA captures learning speed and retention across the stream, unlike ACC which reflects only end-of-stream performance.

Results from Fig. 1(c) and Table 4 show that during the structural-editing procedure (Cycle-TAA), PRUNE achieves higher TAA than GROW at low and intermediate compactness. At $c=20\%$, PRUNE Cycle-TAA is $48.519 \pm 0.348$ vs. GROW $47.288 \pm 0.269$. At $c=30\%$, PRUNE $48.732 \pm 0.358$ vs. GROW $47.871 \pm 0.374$. At $c=40\%$, PRUNE $48.869 \pm 0.251$ vs. GROW $48.338 \pm 0.291$. At $c=50\%$, the two methods are nearly tied: PRUNE $48.997 \pm 0.240$ vs. GROW $48.990 \pm 0.245$.
Welch two-sample t-tests (Table 6) confirm statistical significance at $c=20\%$ ($p < 0.001$), $c=30\%$ ($p = 0.0014$), and $c=40\%$ ($p = 0.0059$), but not at $c=50\%$ ($p = 0.9637$).

Under Winning-Ticket retraining (WT TAA, Fig. 1(d), Table 4), the differences between GROW and PRUNE are not statistically significant at any compactness (Table 6, $p > 0.05$). For example, at $c=20\%$, GROW WT TAA is $46.257 \pm 0.188$ and PRUNE is $46.298 \pm 0.162$; at $c=50\%$, GROW $46.776 \pm 0.174$ and PRUNE $46.749 \pm 0.295$.

The paper concludes that PRUNE achieves higher Cycle-TAA than GROW at low and intermediate compactness during structural editing, while under Winning-Ticket retraining the TAA differences are not significant. This further confirms that the GROW-PRUNE separation lies in adaptive dynamics rather than final architecture quality.

On the CIFAR-100 ConvNet setup (dense convolutional trunk, four-layer FC head, SGD $\eta=0.1$, cosine annealing, 200 epochs, 5 cycles, neutral allocation, ReLU), the paper analyzes event-aligned cohort diagnostics to understand the mechanism behind the GROW-PRUNE asymmetry. For GROW, at each growth cycle $t$, the newborn cohort $\mathcal{N}_t$ is defined as the units activated at that growth step, and the incumbent cohort $\mathcal{O}_t$ as the units already active before that step.

Two signals are measured per unit $j$ on a single mini-batch at the post-growth snapshot: activation rate $\text{act}(j)$, the fraction of post-activation values exceeding a small threshold $\tau$; and per-unit gradient magnitude $\text{grad}(j)$, the mean absolute pre-activation gradient $|\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial z_j|$ where $z_j$ is the unit pre-activation. For linear layers these are averaged over the batch dimension $B$; for convolutional layers, over $(B, H, W)$. Cohort means are computed across units and seeds, and log-parity is defined as $\Delta_{\text{grow,act}}(t,\ell) = \log(\mathbb{E}_{j\in\mathcal{N}_t}[\text{act}(j)] / \mathbb{E}_{j\in\mathcal{O}_t}[\text{act}(j)])$ and similarly for gradient, with parity at 0.
Fig. 2

Results in Fig. 2(a,b) show that at birth, newborn GROW units exhibit positive activation log-parity (log ratio > 0) across compactness levels and cycle indices, indicating that they participate in the forward computation and are not inactive or dead on arrival. However, the same newborn units exhibit strongly negative gradient log-parity (log ratio < 0), indicating that they receive substantially weaker per-unit gradient signal than already-active units.

This demonstrates that the growth bottleneck is a backward-pass integration problem rather than a dead-unit problem: newborn units are forward-active but backward-starved. The current loss is less sensitive to changes through their downstream pathways despite their forward participation.

From the diagnostic analysis (conclusion 5), it was established that newborn units exhibit positive activation log-parity but negative gradient log-parity at birth on CIFAR-100, indicating they are forward-active but backward-starved at the moment of insertion. The paper next asks whether this birth-time asymmetry persists over the subsequent within-cycle training interval.

On the same CIFAR-100 ConvNet setup, the paper tracks newly grown units over the remaining training segment after each growth event. For each cycle, activation ratio $\text{act}_{\text{new}}/\text{act}_{\text{old}}$ and gradient ratio $\text{grad}_{\text{new}}/\text{grad}_{\text{old}}$ are computed across post-insertion training time. Parity is marked by ratio 1.

Results from Fig. 3 show that across compactness levels $c \in \{20,30,40,50\}\%$, the activation ratio (blue curves) stays near parity and sometimes exceeds it, indicating that newborn units approach or exceed forward-activity parity with incumbent units after insertion. In contrast, the gradient ratio (orange curves) remains far below parity throughout the entire cycle, including at the end-of-cycle checkpoint markers.
Fig. 3

The paper concludes that the backward-signal disadvantage is not merely a transient birth-time effect but persists over the available training horizon and limits how quickly newborn units can become useful. Even when newborn units become forward-active, they remain under-integrated in the backward pass, supporting a credit-assignment rather than dead-unit explanation for the growth bottleneck.

Building on the finding that newborn units are forward-active but backward-starved at birth (conclusion 5) and that this backward-signal disadvantage persists throughout the training cycle (conclusion 6), and using the collection of intervention methods evaluated in the previous analysis (conclusion 8), this step examines whether early newborn integration metrics predict Cycle-TAA across all methods and compactness levels.

For each method (vanilla GROW, GROW+TwoSpeed, GROW+MomentTransplant, GROW+Net2Wider, GROW+GradMax, GROW+Rand. Smooth-Leaky, and also Dense and PRUNE baselines) at each compactness level $c \in \{20,30,40,50\}\%$ on CIFAR-100, the paper computes early gradient parity (mean log-ratio of newborn-to-incumbent gradient magnitude over the early post-birth window) and early activation parity (analogous for activation rate). These are correlated with Cycle-TAA using Spearman's rank correlation.

Results from Fig. 4(a,b) show that early gradient parity has a Spearman correlation of $\rho = 0.88$ with Cycle-TAA, and early activation parity has a Spearman correlation of $\rho = 0.83$ with Cycle-TAA. The large labeled markers denote method means across compactness; lighter points show individual compactness/seed-level observations. Methods closer to parity achieve higher Cycle-TAA, with the clearest association observed for gradient parity.
Fig. 4(a,b)

The paper concludes that there is a strong quantitative link between the degree of newborn integration during early post-insertion training and the resulting trajectory-average adaptive performance, supporting that backward credit assignment is the primary newborn-integration bottleneck.

Given the identification of the newborn integration bottleneck (conclusion 5) — specifically that newborn units are forward-active but backward-starved, with the disadvantage persisting through post-birth training (conclusion 6) — the paper evaluates four possible sources of this bottleneck: (i) optimizer state mismatch due to lacking accumulated states, (ii) disruptive insertion operations that perturb the current function, (iii) suboptimal selection of inactive units, and (iv) restricted gradient flow from activation functions.

The following interventions are implemented on the CIFAR-100 ConvNet setup (SGD $\eta=0.1$, cosine annealing, 200 epochs, 5 cycles, neutral allocation). Two-Speed: temporarily multiplies the optimizer update on newborn-associated parameters by a factor $r > 1$ during a warmup window (default $r=5$, $N=1955$ updates), implemented as $W_{\text{slice}} \leftarrow W_{\text{old,slice}} + r (W_{\text{new,slice}} - W_{\text{old,slice}})$. Moment Transplant: copies optimizer buffers (e.g., momentum and variance estimates under adaptive optimizers) from a matched active donor unit into the newborn unit. Net2Wider: implements function-preserving widening by duplicating selected incumbent units and redistributing outgoing weights so the network function is initially unchanged. GradMax: scores inactive candidates by the learning signal they would receive on the mini-batch at the growth event, activating the top-$k$ units. Rand. Smooth-Leaky: replaces the standard ReLU activation with a smoother randomized leaky activation designed to preserve non-zero gradient flow.

All intervention methods are evaluated on CIFAR-100 under the same training protocol. The primary metric is Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during structural editing), and early integration parity (activation and gradient log-ratios in the early post-birth window) is measured to assess how well newborn units integrate.

Results from Fig. 4 (panels a-b) show that GradMax-style gradient-based selection and Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation achieve the highest early integration parity and the highest Cycle-TAA among the evaluated interventions. Two-Speed and Net2Wider provide weaker or less consistent relief across compactness levels. Moment Transplant provides intermediate gains. For example, the labeled markers in Fig. 4 indicate that GradMax and Rand. Smooth-Leaky occupy the upper-right region (higher parity, higher Cycle-TAA), while Two-Speed and Net2Wider are further from parity.
Fig. 4

The paper concludes that among the evaluated interventions targeting the newborn integration bottleneck, GradMax-style gradient-based selection and Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation achieve the highest early integration parity and Cycle-TAA, demonstrating that improving the integration of newborn units can strengthen adaptive-process performance, with selection policy and activation-level trainability being the most effective levers among those tested.

From the intervention study (conclusion 8), we have measurements of Cycle-TAA (edit-time integration metric) and Winning-Ticket accuracy (final mask quality) for each method on CIFAR-100 at compactness levels $c \in \{20,30,40,50\}\%$. This step examines the relationship between these two evaluation axes across interventions.

Results from Fig. 4(c) show that Winning-Ticket accuracy is not monotonically aligned with Cycle-TAA across interventions. Methods that substantially improve edit-time integration (such as GradMax or Rand. Smooth-Leaky, which achieve high Cycle-TAA) do not necessarily produce better final retrainable subnetworks; in some cases their Winning-Ticket accuracy is similar to or lower than that of methods with lower Cycle-TAA.
Fig. 4(c)

The paper concludes that better edit-time integration does not guarantee better final masks. This decoupling shows that improved edit-time dynamics and final architecture quality are distinct objectives that may require separate optimization criteria.

The intervention study (conclusion 8) on CIFAR-100 identified Rand. Smooth-Leaky as an effective intervention for improving newborn integration in the adaptive-cycle setting. This motivates testing whether growth with improved integration can be competitive in a continual learning setting with sequential class accumulation, where structural edits are separated by more optimization time.

The paper evaluates class-incremental Split-CIFAR100: CIFAR-100 is partitioned into a sequence of disjoint class-incremental tasks. All methods use a shared classifier head with no task-identity routing. At each task boundary, structural edits occur before continuing optimization on the new task. This regime gives each structural edit substantially more optimization time before the next shift compared to the repeated-shift settings.

The following methods are compared: DENSE (no sparsification), PRUNE (IMP with rewind), vanilla GROW, and GROW combined with various birth interventions: TwoSpeed, MomentTransplant, GradMax, Net2Wider, and Rand. Smooth-Leaky. Learning rates are selected per method and benchmark from the set {0.01, 0.001, 0.0001} based on best average accuracy.

Results from Fig. 5 (also Table 14) show that GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation outperforms DENSE, PRUNE, and all other growth variants (vanilla GROW, GROW+TwoSpeed, GROW+MomentTransplant, GROW+GradMax, GROW+Net2Wider) in final accuracy across compactness levels. For example, at c=20%, GROW+Rand. Smooth-Leaky achieves average accuracy 25.0±0.7 compared to PRUNE 21.3±0.6, DENSE 15.8±0.5, and vanilla GROW 19.8±1.2 (Table 14). Vanilla GROW remains weak.
Fig. 5

The paper concludes that in a sequential class-incremental setting with substantial optimization time between edits, GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation outperforms all other methods, demonstrating that growth can be a competitive alternative to pruning in continual learning settings when newborn units have enough optimization time to integrate and are made more trainable through activation-level intervention.

The intervention study (conclusion 8) compared several growth variants on CIFAR-100. To further test their effectiveness under repeated distribution shifts that stress plasticity, the paper evaluates these methods on five plasticity-stressing continual learning benchmarks: Permuted MNIST (500 tasks, 10,000 images/task, 1 epoch/task), Random Label MNIST (50 tasks, 1,200 images/task, 400 epochs/task), Random Label CIFAR (50 tasks, 1,200 images/task, 400 epochs/task), 5+1 CIFAR (15 tasks alternating hard/easy, 780 timesteps/task), and Continual ImageNet (500 binary tasks, 1,200 images/task, 10 epochs/task). These benchmarks feature rapid distribution change with limited integration time per task.

Methods compared include DENSE, PRUNE, vanilla GROW, and GROW with birth interventions (TwoSpeed, MomentTransplant, GradMax, Net2Wider, Rand. Smooth-Leaky). Learning rates are selected per benchmark and method from {0.01, 0.001, 0.0001}. Performance is measured using average accuracy or TAOA (Total Average Online Accuracy) and Early Task TAA.

Results from Fig. 5 and Table 14 show that PRUNE is the strongest or near-strongest structural baseline across these rapid-shift settings. For example, on Permuted MNIST at c=20%, PRUNE achieves 85.9±0.1 average accuracy vs. vanilla GROW 71.5±0.1 and GROW+Rand. Smooth-Leaky 75.1±0.1; on Continual ImageNet at c=20%, PRUNE 89.9±0.3 vs. GROW 70.7±1.1 and GROW+Rand. Smooth-Leaky 81.5±0.1.

Among growth-family methods, GROW + Rand. Smooth-Leaky is the most robust: it consistently improves over vanilla GROW, narrows the gap to PRUNE, and is the only growth variant that becomes competitive with or outperforms PRUNE in settings where structural events are separated by more optimization time (Split-CIFAR100). Other birth interventions (Two-Speed, Moment Transplant, GradMax, Net2Wider) provide less consistent gains across this benchmark suite.

The paper concludes that under rapid distribution change with limited integration time, PRUNE is reliable due to preserving mature capacity, while GROW+Rand. Smooth-Leaky is the most robust growth variant, consistently improving over vanilla GROW and narrowing the gap to PRUNE.

open_questions.content: The results of this paper suggest that structural adaptation should be evaluated not only by the architectures it produces, but also by the optimization compatibility of the edits used to produce them. Several scientifically meaningful unresolved issues remain. First, the growth rules examined in this work are static heuristics (activation-frequency scoring, gradient-based scoring) applied at predetermined edit intervals; an open question is how to design policies that respond to real-time newborn-integration signals—such as current gradient parity or activation ratio—to decide adaptively when and where to grow, and how to give new structure a realistic chance to integrate based on the current state of the optimization trajectory. Second, this study was restricted to unit-level structural edits in the fully-connected head of a hybrid ConvNet on CIFAR-scale datasets; generalizing these findings to architectures where structural edits act more directly on learned representations (e.g., convolutional filters, transformer attention heads, or residual blocks) and to larger-scale problems such as ImageNet-scale classification or language modeling remains open. Third, the continual learning experiments were conducted with known task boundaries in single-head class-incremental and repeated-shift settings; testing these ideas in task-agnostic continual learning settings—where the model must detect distribution shift without explicit boundaries and decide autonomously when to expand—is a natural next step. Fourth, the observation that edit-time integration and final architecture quality are decoupled raises the question of whether growth-based structural plasticity can be optimized for both objectives simultaneously, or whether separate mechanisms are required. Fifth, the mechanism by which Rand. Smooth-Leaky improves newborn activation-level trainability operates through activation-level gradient flow, but the exact pathway—whether through reduced saturation, smoother loss landscape, or improved gradient propagation through depth—remains to be identified. Finally, the interaction between growth frequency, inter-edit training duration, and newborn integration time scale was investigated under a fixed total training horizon; designing growth schedules that optimally allocate integration time across edits in resource-constrained settings is an open design problem.
